comment: Potica Notebook entry bank. potica-pulse.yml publishes entries[nextIndex] into notebook.html every 5 days, then increments nextIndex. Every entry was fact-checked 2026-07-03/04 against the sources cited on about-potica.html and the guides. Refill by appending entries — never edit published ones here.

entries.title: Only five fillings are legally 'Slovenska potica'
entries.body: Under EU Regulation 2021/656, a potica sold as protected "Slovenska potica" may contain exactly five fillings: walnut, walnut with raisins, raisin, tarragon, or tarragon with cottage cheese. Everything else is delicious — but it isn't the protected article. The full specification →

entries.title: Potica's first appearance in print was a complaint
entries.body: The earliest written record of potica comes from Primož Trubar's catechism writings of 1575 and 1577 — the reformer who gave Slovenian its first printed book also disapproved, in print, of women offering potice as votive gifts. The pastry was already so embedded in folk life that it made it into theology. More →

entries.title: 1689: the first full description
entries.body: Janez Vajkard Valvasor's encyclopedic Glory of the Duchy of Carniola (1689) gave the first detailed description of potica — thin dough coated with honey and walnuts, tightly rolled — a recipe that mirrors the modern walnut potica almost exactly, three and a half centuries later. More →

entries.title: The hole in the pan is engineering, not decoration
entries.body: The potičnik's central cone turns one of the densest loaves in home baking into a ring, so oven heat attacks from the inside and the outside at once. No cold core, no doughy centre. The EU spec requires the pan for protected Slovenska potica — minimum 14 cm across. The pan guide →

entries.title: The newspaper test
entries.body: In potica and povitica kitchens on two continents, the folk benchmark for dough is the same: stretched thin enough to read a newspaper through. Iron Range grandmothers held it up to the light; Kansas City's Croatian bakers still describe it the same way. How to get there →

entries.title: Potica is better on day two — plan for it
entries.body: Fresh from the oven is the wrong day to judge a potica. Overnight, moisture migrates from the filling into the crumb and the flavours knit. Bakers deliberately bake a day ahead. If your schedule allows the rest day, take it. Storing guide →

entries.title: The Iron Range's potica institution was founded by a Roman
entries.body: Sunrise Bakery in Hibbing, Minnesota, was founded in 1913 by Giulio Forti, a scratch baker from Rome. Potica entered the family in 1932, when Forti's son married the daughter of Croatian immigrants — and a 1991 Los Angeles Times mention later set the mail-order phones ringing. The Iron Range's intermarried food history, in one bakery. Potica in America →

entries.title: The Three P's
entries.body: On Minnesota's Iron Range, three miners' foods crossed every ethnic line and became the region's shared table: potica (Slovenian), pasties (Cornish), and porketta (Italian). You don't have to be Slovenian to bake potica on the Range — it stopped being ethnic food and became Ranger food. The full story →

entries.title: Same pastry, older name
entries.body: Kansas City's Croatian community never shortened the word: there it is povitica, and the Strawberry Hill Baking Company has made it commercially since 1984 — a fourth generation of the family bakes it today. In Slovenia the same word wore down to potica. The naming story →

entries.title: The name is the instruction
entries.body: Potica comes from the Slovenian verb poviti — to wrap, to roll up. The older form povitica contracted as the pastry became Slovenia's national dish. Everything the pastry is — thin dough, filling to the edges, the tight spiral — lives inside that one verb. Etymology →

entries.title: Potica has been served in the United States Senate
entries.body: Senator Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota — Slovenian on her Iron Range side — has served potica to colleagues in Washington, where it reportedly won fans on both sides of the aisle. From a miner's steamer trunk to the Capitol in about a century. More →

entries.title: The cookbook written for readers with no grandmother left to ask
entries.body: Woman's Glory — The Kitchen, published by the Slovenian Women's Union of America for its silver anniversary (1926–1951), was compiled — in editor Albina Novak's words — as an "instructor" for women who wished to make "dishes for which their mothers have always been famous." A survival document disguised as a cookbook. More →

entries.title: Whole poppy seeds taste like almost nothing
entries.body: They are sealed capsules — baked whole, they stay gritty and bland. Ground, they release their oils and become the dark, fragrant paste the pastry is named for. If a poppy seed roll ever disappointed you, this step was probably skipped. Poppy seed potica →

entries.title: Toast the walnuts. Then wait.
entries.body: Eight minutes at 160 °C deepens walnut flavour dramatically — but grind them warm and they smear into oily paste. Cold, brittle nuts shatter cleanly into the coarse-sand texture a potica filling wants. The waiting is part of the recipe. Grinding guide →

entries.title: The tarragon one is not a novelty
entries.body: Pehtranova potica — sweet tarragon potica — is one of the five EU-protected fillings and a long-standing Easter bake, cherished especially around Novo mesto in Dolenjska. Sweet herb pastry sounds like a modern stunt; it is one of the oldest ideas in the repertoire. Tarragon potica →

entries.title: December 2021: national heritage status
entries.body: Potica-making entered Slovenia's national register of intangible cultural heritage in December 2021 — the same year "Slovenska potica" received EU Traditional Speciality Guaranteed protection. Legal recognition, twice over, for a farmhouse pastry. The history →

entries.title: Three to four turns, by law
entries.body: The EU specification for protected Slovenska potica requires at least three to four full turns of dough and filling in the finished loaf — which is only physically possible when the dough is rolled genuinely thin. The spiral count is the honesty meter. Rolling guide →

entries.title: The two-second test that predicts your whole bake
entries.body: Pinch off a piece of kneaded dough and stretch it slowly. If it forms a thin translucent membrane before tearing — the windowpane — your gluten will survive being rolled to 3 mm. If it tears immediately, keep kneading. Two seconds now saves an hour of frustration later. The dough, explained →

entries.title: Orehnjača and makovnjača
entries.body: Croatia names the roll for its filling: orehnjača from oreh (walnut), makovnjača from mak (poppy). Same family as potica and povitica — the name on the table tells you which village the recipe walked out of. The family tree →

entries.title: The cousins: bejgli and makowiec
entries.body: Hungary rolls poppy and walnut bejgli at Christmas; Poland bakes makowiec. Both are branches of the same Central European rolled-yeast-bread family as potica — overlapping cousins, each certain theirs is the original. Compare them →

entries.title: "One village, one potica"
entries.body: The Slovenian folk proverb captures the pastry's real taxonomy: estimates run to dozens upon dozens of distinct regional varieties — sweet, savory, walnut, tarragon, even crackling-filled. The walnut potica you know is the ambassador, not the whole country. The varieties →

entries.title: Freeze it by the slice
entries.body: Potica freezes exceptionally well — its density is an asset. The connoisseur's move: freeze individual slices on a tray, bag them, and pull one at a time with coffee for the rest of winter. Thaw wrapped, so the condensation lands on the wrapper instead of the crumb. Storing guide →

entries.title: Revna potica — the poor man's roll
entries.body: Not every potica was a celebration of abundance. The revna (poor) potica stretched scarce filling across the same devoted dough — proof that the form mattered as much as the fortune behind it. The spiral was the point. More varieties →

entries.title: Potica once paid taxes
entries.body: Historical records from Valvasor's era indicate a potica was sometimes accepted as partial payment of taxes in Carniola. A pastry with enough standing to settle debts to the state — in the 17th century. The history →
